Learning Objectives
Perform an appropriate workup for patients in whom metastatic disease in the pelvis is
suspected.
Review the surgical and nonsurgical management of metastatic disease in the pelvis.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
Each year, metastatic disease to bone will develop in one-half of patients diagnosed with a new
cancer.
The pelvis is the second-most common site for bony metastatic disease.

Epidemiology
Metastatic bone disease frequently is observed in patients with carcinomas (namely,
breast, lung, prostate, thyroid, and renal cell). The bony pelvis is a common location for
metastatic disease, accounting for 40% of all cases in bone.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
During weight bearing, the pelvis transfers forces of the lower extremity to the spine.
The pelvis is divided into zones based on the Enneking classification (Figure 1)
Type I: iliac
Type II: periacetabular
Type III: ischiopubic
Type IV: sacral

Biomechanics
A tumor’s location determines its biomechanical effect.
The pelvis is divided into weight-bearing and non weight-bearing zones.
Weight bearing: axis from the femur through the acetabulum and through the pelvic
columns to the sacroiliac joint and sacrum
Posterior column, anterior column, superior dome of the acetabulum, sacroiliac joint
Non-weight bearing: iliac wing, anterior acetabulum, ischiopubic

Biomechanics
The bony pelvis is the structural connection between the lower extremities and the axial
skeleton, transferring forces of weight bearing through an axis that runs from the femur
and acetabulum through the pelvic columns to the sacroiliac joint. Primary oncologic
resections of the pelvis are divided into zones according to the Enneking classification
system (Figure 1); however, this system also is useful in the metastatic setting. Pelvic
resections are demanding, and all preoperative images must be analyzed to determine
the location of the tumor in relation to the relevant pelvic anatomy, especially important
vascular and neurologic structures. The zones of the pelvis also help determine
treatment options for patients and indicate the biomechanical implications of a

weight-bearing portion of the pelvis will determine if reconstruction is necessary.1
Risk Factors
Metastasis to bone often originates from breast, prostate, thyroid, renal, and lung carcinomas.

Acetabular Bone Loss
Metastatic tumors that develop in the weight-bearing zones of the pelvis (ie, the
anterior/posterior column, superior dome of the pelvis, and sacroiliac joint) are
approached in a different manner than tumors that occur in the non-weight-bearing
zones of the pelvis (ie, iliac wing, ischiopubic, anterior acetabulum). The acetabulum is a
common location of metastatic disease. The Harrington classification system (Resource
1) and the Metastatic Acetabular Classification System ( Figure 2) often are used to
describe the location of these tumors and to help plan surgical mangaement.3

Patient History
Pain patterns may help localize tumors and determine the need for management.
Progressive pain that occurs at rest and with weight bearing
Weight-bearing pain may indicate the tumor is in the weight-bearing axis of the pelvis.
Similar to hip arthritis, groin pain may indicate an acetabular or femoral head tumor.
Pain in the thigh should always be evaluated for concurrent femoral metastatic disease.
Evaluate for a patient history of primary cancers and metastatic disease
Evaluate for a patient history of radiation therapy to the pelvis
Physical Examination
Occasional swelling, a limp, or pain with hip range of motion
Pain when rising from a chair
Neurovascular Examination
Sciatic and femoral nerve examinations showing a deficit should be documented
preoperatively.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographic workup
Plain radiographs of the pelvis and hip
AP pelvis, AP hip, cross-table lateral views
Cross-table lateral view helpful in evaluating the posterior column
Judet views
Assess the anterior and posterior columns and acetabular walls, dome of the acetabulum,
and the quadrilateral plate.
Femur
Obtain AP and lateral views of the entire ipsilateral femur.
Computed Tomography
A CT scan of the pelvis may help assess bony destruction of the acetabulum.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI often is unnecessary for evaluation of known metastatic disease.
May be helpful to assess intrapelvic soft-tissue involvement
Useful for evaluating a stress-related fracture of the acetabulum secondary to previous
radiation
If primary pelvic malignancy is a concern, MRI is useful for evaluating tumor location/extent
and planning a biopsy.
Bone Scintigraphy
May be helpful if a primary tumor is suspected and to evaluate for other sites of bony disease
Positron Emission Tomography
Useful if concern for a primary tumor exists and to evaluate for other sites of disease
Positron emission tomography avidity often overestimates the amount of bony destruction.

Most common forms of metastatic disease to bone
Breast, thyroid, renal, lung, and prostate carcinomas
Hematologic malignancies
Myeloma and lymphoma
Primary bone tumors are common in the pelvis.
Affected age group is similar to that of patients with metastatic disease to bone.
Chondrosarcoma
Radiation-associated sarcomas
Osteosarcoma
Paget’s sarcoma

Diagnosis
Patients with a new pelvic bone tumor, an isolated tumor, and no known history of bony
metastatic disease should undergo a biopsy before treatment.
Common scenarios
Patient with a known history of carcinoma with multiple bony or visceral/nodal metastases:
often does not require biopsy
Patient with a known history of carcinoma and an isolated bone lesion but no history of bony
metastases: requires a biopsy
Patient with a known history of carcinoma and hip/groin pain with normal radiographs: may
be symptomatic from other treatment options, such as diphosphonates or chemotherapy
May consider MRI of the pelvis to evaluate for stress reaction or radiographically occult
tumor
Patient older than 40 years with a new pelvic lesion: must undergo a biopsy before surgical
treatment
Differential Diagnosis
In patients older than 40 years, most commonly because of metastatic disease, myeloma, and
lymphoma
Primary tumors in the pelvis, namely chondrosarcoma, are common in this age group.
Benign conditions such as Paget disease and hyperparathyroidism

Differential Diagnosis
In patients with bony metastatic disease, a workup is essential1,4 (Resource 2). Patients
with a known carcinoma who have multiple bony lesions are approached differently than
patients with a solitary bony lesion (even in the setting of known carcinoma). During the
patient history and physical examination, localization of pain often helps identify the
position of the tumor (eg, groin pain for acetabular disease) and indicates if the lesion
has compromised the structure of the pelvis (eg, pain with weight bearing). Plain
radiographs typically are the first imaging studies obtained to evaluate patients with
metastatic disease and often are adequate to pinpoint the tumor and identify potential
biomechanical implications. Orthogonal radiographs of the affected femur also are

important to identify any other metastatic deposits. CT and MRI may be useful to gauge
the extent of bony destruction and the size of any soft-tissue masses, whereas bone
scintigraphy or positron emission tomography and CT may reveal other sites of bony
disease.
Diagnosis of lesions is essential before management is planned. Although most patients
older than 45 years with a lytic bony lesion have metastatic disease, myeloma, or
lymphoma, primary malignances, namely chondrosarcoma, also are observed in this age
group. Therefore, the workup for an isolated bony lesion, even in patients with a known
history of carcinoma, should include a biopsy.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Important factors in the management of metastatic pelvic disease include histologic diagnosis,
amount of bony destruction, candidacy for surgical treatment, and expected prognosis.
In all patients with metastatic disease in the pelvis, a trial of radiation therapy, medical
management, and protected–weight bearing should be considered.
This treatment is relatively contraindicated in patients with protrusio acetabular defects or
pelvic discontinuity.
Nondisplaced fractures (depending on location)
Treatment-naive patients with breast carcinoma, lymphoma, or myeloma
Typically respond well to medical management
Non–weight-bearing locations of the pelvis
Nonacetabular lesions
Poor medical health/shortened life span
Techniques/Procedures
Observation/pain management
Painless weight bearing with the assistance of a walker, cane, or crutches
Pain management is important in all symptomatic patients.

Opioids
Nonopioids: NSAIDs, tricyclic antidepressants, muscle relaxants, and steroids
A bowel program is necessary to prevent severe constipation.
Epidural catheters
Effective for pain management in patients with end-stage disease
Medical management
Chemotherapy/hormone management/growth factor-receptor inhibitors
Depends on tumor histology
Diphosphonates and denosumab
Reduce pain and skeletal-related events
May be associated with hypocalcemia and osteonecrosis of the jaw
Radiation
External beam radiation
Indications: painful or progressive lesions
Dose: usually 30 Gy in 10 fractions or 20 Gy in five fractions to bone lesion (may use
higher dose/fewer fractions)
Data show high-dose/low-fraction radiation therapy techniques are effective for more
radioresistant histologies (renal cell carcinoma).5
One dose of 8 Gy is effective for palliative pain relief; however, retreatment rates are
higher.
Minimally invasive techniques
Consider these techniques in patients who are not medically fit for surgical treatment.
Radiofrequency ablation or cryoablation
Provides local tumor control via thermal necrosis
Often combined with cementoplasty and percutaneous fixation
Allows for immediate weight bearing and offers reliable pain relief

Nonsurgical Management
In patients with metastatic disease involving the pelvis, treatment is designed to balance
maximal function with essential medical management for their survival. For most
patients with metastatic pelvic disease, nonsurgical treatment options are initiated first
(relative contraindications to nonsurgical management include pelvic discontinuity and

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001040
15/31

protrusio acetabular defects). These measures often involve a trial of radiation therapy,
pain management, diphosphonates, chemotherapy/immunotherapy, and protected–
weight bearing. In patients with a tumor involving non-weight-bearing portions of the
pelvis, this may be definitive treatment. In patients with a tumor in a weight-bearing
portion of the acetabulum, additional nonsurgical treatment options, such as
radiofrequency ablation or cryotherapy, may be combined with cementoplasty and
limited fixation to allow for immediate–weight bearing.
Surgical Management
Goals of surgical management
Relieve pain
Allow for unrestricted and immediate–weight bearing
Restore force transmission from the lower extremity through the pelvic columns to the
sacrum and spine
Often dictated by tumor location
Nonacetabular versus acetabular tumors
Indications
Nonacetabular tumors
Failed nonsurgical management
Acetabular tumors
Failed nonsurgical management
Pelvic discontinuity
Protusio deformity of the femoral head
Costs associated with care
In patients with metastatic disease, the cost of care is substantially reduced for those
undergoing surgical treatment compared with those undergoing nonsurgical treatment.
Surgical treatment allows patients to maintain ambulatory status, whereas nonsurgical
treatment may keep patients non-weight bearing.
Contraindications

Patients who are not medically fit for a surgical procedure
Functional status, activity, disease status
Patients who require continued chemotherapeutics because of disease status

Contraindications
Although patients often respond well to nonsurgical treatment, especially those with
certain treatment-naive histologies (ie, breast carcinoma, lymphoma, and myeloma) and
tumors in non?weight-bearing portions of the acetabulum, patients with tumors
involving weight-bearing structures of the acetabulum often proceed directly to surgical
treatment. The goal of surgical treatment is immediate and unrestricted weight bearing.
The ability to keep patients weight bearing and consequently avoid admission to a step-
down or care facility substantially reduces the cost of care. Postoperatively, patients
often are treated with adjuvant medical therapies and radiation therapy to reduce the
risk of disease recurrence/progression.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Preoperative considerations
Preoperative embolization for highly vascular lesions
Patients with a history of renal cell and thyroid carcinoma
Surgical management should be performed within 48 to 72 hours (approximately 3 days) of
embolization.
Discussion with an interventional radiologist to avoid embolization of gluteal vessels, which
provide blood to the soft-tissue flap/skin
Necrosis of a skin flap may be a devastating complication, leading to major wound healing
and infection complications (Figure 3).

Patients should discontinue any chemotherapeutics that will increase the risk of bleeding,
infection, or deep vein thrombosis (DVT)/pulmonary embolism.
Vascular endothelial growth factor-targeted agents and tyrosine kinase inhibitors
Patients should take a 6- to 8-week drug holiday preoperatively, followed by a 4- to 6-week

Inferior vena cava filter placement

The surgical approach and plan should be determined preoperatively to expedite the
procedure and decrease the risk of infection because of a prolonged surgical procedure.
The surgical approach is based on the tumor location.

Patient Positioning
Depending on treatment modality, consider using a radiolucent table to accommodate
fluoroscopy.
Supine position
With nonacetabular tumors involving the anterior ring
Rolling sloppy lateral position
If concomitant approach to the anterior and posterior rings is necessary
Utilitarian pelvic incision
Lateral decubitus position
Standard total hip arthroplasty approach, depending on surgeon preference
If a Harrington technique is planned, include the iliac brim and ischium to allow for pin
placement.
Surgical Approaches
Nonacetabular tumors
Extended intralesional curettage
Use of mechanical (high-speed burr), chemical (phenol or hydrogen peroxide), and thermal
(cryotherapy, argon beam electrocoagulator, cautery on spray) adjuvants
Augmentation with polymethyl methacrylate
Acetabular tumors
Goal is to transmit the forces of the hip to the intact posterior pelvis (sacroiliac joint)
The extent and the location of bone destruction delineate the treatment options.
All gross tumors should be removed via extended intralesional curettage with or without
adjuvants.
Femoral fixation depends on disease status.
Cemented implants commonly are used.
Noncemented acetabular components (Figure 4)
Trabecular metal acetabular components and augments with multiple screws into the
intact bone
Highly porous augments are used to fill bone defects.

Harrington technique: type of fixation and hip arthroplasty dependent on defect location
Should use fully threaded Steinmann pins or screws
Type I: defect does not compromise fixation of a standard cemented total hip

Type II: lack of medial wall support for a standard hip arthroplasty

Type V: may be considered for resection arthroplasty and a custom or cone prosthesis
For exposure, a constrained liner may be considered in patients with notable soft-tissue

Saddle and periacetabular endoprostheses may be considered in patients with a large, type

Associated with elevated risk of complications
Designed to allow for flexion and extension

Postoperative Management
Most pelvic tumors respond to nonsurgical management; however, if nonsurgical
management fails, surgical management of pelvic metastatic disease is indicated to
allow resumption of weight bearing and avoid the complications and costs associated
with bed rest. Careful preoperative planning and medical optimization are paramount
for good patient outcomes. Patients need to stop chemotherapeutics and
immunotherapies preoperatively. In patients with a highly vascular tumor (ie, renal cell
and thyroid carcinoma, some plasmacytomas) or large intrapelvic soft-tissue masses,
preoperative arterial embolization is indicated, and surgical management should take
place within 72 hours (ideally, within 24 hours) of the procedure. The tumor location
often dictates the surgical approach and plan. In patients with a refractory, non-weight-
bearing tumor, extended intralesional curettage and cement fixation often is the
preferred treatment optoin.7,8 In patients with a tumor involving the weight-bearing axis
of the pelvis, namely acetabular disease, the goal is to provide solid fixation between the
deficient acetabulum and the remaining ilium/sacroiliac joints.9-11 Both cemented and
noncemented total hip arthroplasty constructs have shown excellent durability and pain
relief in this patient population (Resource 3).
The cemented Harrington technique and its modifications are most often used to
provide structural stabilization of the acetabulum (Resources 4 and 5). New
noncemented techniques with the use of highly porous tantalum acetabular
components and augments also are a durable means of fixation, even in patients who
have undergone previous radiation therapy (Resource 6). With both methods, multiple
pins or screws are required to provide fixation in the remaining host bone, with ischial
fixation being a key to construct rigidity. In patients with extreme acetabular bone loss,
custom or cone prostheses may be used. Although pelvic endoprostheses also are
available, these implants are considered historic options because of the high incidence
of complications associated with their use. Minimally invasive options using trauma
principles also have been described, namely the tripod technique (Resource 7). In this

Complications
Nonunion
Because active disease and radiation/systematic therapy variables typically are present, bony
healing is unreliable; this must be considered in selectin of the reconstruction construct.
Pain
Multimodal pain regimens allow for weight bearing on the surgical extremity.
Patients have substantial improvement in pain and function postoperatively.
Palliative medicine partners should be involved in the treatment of patients with cancer and
postoperative pain.
Infection
A high rate of infection has been observed in patients undergoing an endoprosthesis
reconstruction.
Wound healing complications are associated with the use of vascular endothelial growth factor
inhibitors.
Implant Failure
The incidence of acetabular component loosening is low.
In cemented and noncemented reconstructions
Often because of tumor progression rather than to structural failure of the implant
